title: Tea May Benefit Heart Health — If It's Not Too Hot
paragraphs: Regular tea drinking may be linked to a lower risk of heart disease and stroke, according to a new study from China. But how hot you drink it could matter, too!

Researchers looked at data from almost 486,000 people in China aged between 30 and 79. Participants reported how often they drank tea, which type they preferred, how strong they brewed it and how hot they drank it.
The study, published in the Journal of Internal Medicine, tracked their health for an average of nine years.
People who drank tea on at least three days a week had an 11% lower risk of vascular disease — including heart disease and stroke — than those who drank it less often.
The link remained after the researchers considered factors such as age, smoking, physical activity, body weight and existing health conditions.
Black tea was more consistently associated with a lower risk of vascular disease than green tea, although both were associated with benefits. Moderate-strength tea was also linked with a lower risk.

However, those who described their tea as "burning hot" had a 16% higher risk of vascular disease than people who did not regularly drink tea. The temperatures were reported by participants, rather than measured by the researchers.
Tea contains polyphenols, which may help explain these findings. These plant compounds may help reduce inflammation, protect the cells lining blood vessels and keep arteries working well.
However, the study doesn't prove that tea caused the differences in risk. Other differences in people's diets and lifestyles could help explain the results.

In fact, the lowest risk of vascular disease was found among regular tea drinkers who also did not smoke and had high levels of physical activity. So although tea may have benefits for your health, it should be considered just one part of a generally healthy lifestyle.
